tagline: Africa's longest coastline, poets and camels
overview:
Somalia occupies the Horn of Africa, the pointed cape that juts into the Indian Ocean beside the mouth of the Red Sea. It has the longest coastline of any country on mainland Africa, roughly 3,300 kilometers, and covers an area a little smaller than Texas. Mogadishu, the capital, is an ancient Indian Ocean trading port of white buildings and long beaches, slowly rebuilt after years of fighting.

About 18 million people live in Somalia, and they share one language, Somali, alongside Arabic; almost everyone is Muslim, which makes the country unusually united in language and faith. Somalia is a federal republic. Many families are nomadic or semi-nomadic, moving herds of camels, goats and sheep between wells and pastures, and Somalia keeps more camels than any other country on Earth. Decades of conflict have made life hard, yet livestock trade, money sent home by Somalis living abroad, and a fast mobile-phone industry keep the economy moving.
landAndNature: Most of Somalia is hot, dry plain and thorny scrub. In the north the Golis and Cal Madow ranges rise above the Gulf of Aden to about 2,400 meters, catching enough sea mist to support pockets of juniper forest. Only two permanent rivers, the Jubba and the Shabelle, flow down from the Ethiopian highlands and water the farmland of the south. Rains arrive in two seasons, gu and deyr, and when they fail, drought follows quickly. Frankincense and myrrh trees, whose fragrant resin has been traded for thousands of years, grow on the northern cliffs. Wildlife includes the Somali wild ass, the long-necked gerenuk antelope, and many birds found nowhere else.
peopleAndCulture: Somalis call their country a nation of poets. Poems are composed aloud, memorized and recited at gatherings, and a well-made verse can settle an argument or make a reputation. Family lineages are recited too, tracing ancestors back many generations. Camel milk, rice with goat, and anjero, a spongy sourdough pancake, are everyday foods, and bananas are often eaten alongside rice. Tea is spiced with cardamom and cinnamon. Somali has been written in the Latin alphabet only since 1972. Soccer and basketball are popular, music with the oud and drums accompanies weddings, and intricate henna patterns are painted on hands for celebrations.
history: Somali lands traded with Egypt, Arabia, Persia and China for thousands of years, and coastal cities such as Mogadishu and Zeila grew rich on incense, cloth and gold. Islam arrived early, carried across the Red Sea. In the 1800s Britain and Italy divided the region into colonies, and the two parts joined at independence on July 1, 1960. A military government under Siad Barre took power in 1969 and collapsed in 1991, leaving no working national government and beginning decades of civil war, famine and piracy at sea. In 1991 the northwest declared itself the Republic of Somaliland; it governs itself but is not widely recognized by other countries. A federal government was re-established in 2012, and rebuilding continues.
funFacts: Somalia keeps more camels than any other country, roughly seven million, and camel milk is an ordinary everyday drink.
Somali was given an official written alphabet only in 1972, after which a nationwide campaign taught people to read it.
Frankincense, burned in temples since ancient Egypt, still comes largely from trees growing on Somalia's northern hillsides.
The caves of Laas Geel hold vivid rock paintings of long-horned cattle made as much as 5,000 years ago.
Somalia's coastline, about 3,300 kilometers long, is the longest of any country on the African mainland.
